title: Position-table proportional control
physicalPurpose: Move a payload carriage to a commanded angular position without exceeding motor torque limits.
principalTechnique: Proportional position feedback and stiffness-damping trade-off
objective: Tune a proportional position controller experimentally and explain why increasing position stiffness eventually causes unacceptable overshoot, oscillation, and motor effort.

simplifications: The table and payload are represented by one rigid rotational inertia.
Gear elasticity, backlash, encoder noise and Coulomb friction are deferred to later lessons.

baseline.limitation: Low proportional stiffness reaches the target slowly; increasing gain is the obvious next experiment.

change.decision: Change only proportional gain and reject the faster candidate if its overshoot, oscillation or peak torque is unacceptable.

abortPredicates: Position, velocity or torque is nonfinite
Applied torque leaves -10 to 10 N m
simulationOnlyRestrictions: Simulation results do not qualify a physical axis, payload, drive or emergency-stop system.

video.viewerOutcome: Explain proportional position stiffness and use rise time, overshoot, oscillation and torque evidence to reject excessive gain.

learning.context: A motor-driven positioning table must move a payload to a commanded angle while an encoder measures position and a drive applies bounded motor torque.
learning.reason: The thermal lessons established process control; this faster inertial plant shows why proportional gain also changes mechanical stiffness, speed and damping.
theory: The setpoint (SP) is the desired table angle and the process value (PV) is the encoder-measured angle; both use radians.

The error (e) is the setpoint minus the process value. The requested motor torque (T_requested) is the controller calculation before the drive limit, and the applied motor torque (T_applied) is the plant input after that limit; both use newton metres.

The proportional gain (Kp) states the requested motor torque per radian of position error, so T_requested = Kp times e and proportional feedback behaves like a virtual spring. The undamped natural frequency (omega_n) is the oscillation rate in radians per second and equals the square root of Kp divided by inertia J for this rigid table.
Inertia resists acceleration and viscous friction opposes velocity. Natural response and damping describe how the table rises, overshoots and oscillates.
The 90-percent rise time is the first time PV reaches 0.9 rad, position overshoot is maximum PV minus SP, and peak applied torque is maximum absolute T_applied over the complete run.
learning.workedPrediction: A one-radian initial error requests 2 N m at Kp 2 and 8 N m at Kp 8. Predict the higher gain to reach the target sooner while producing more overshoot and torque.
practicalPreparation: Confirm zero initial position and velocity, one-radian step, 20 ms cycle, plus or minus 10 N m torque limit and zero-torque safe state.
Retain position, velocity, torque, gain, timing, limits and simulation evidence for two fresh equivalent runs.
learning.baseline: Run proportional gain 2 from the declared initial state and record 90-percent rise time, overshoot and peak torque.
learning.change: Use one reviewed ExperimentEnabled authority to make the project configure proportional gain 8, execute the selected one-radian move, and restore gain 2 with Manual zero torque.
learning.comparison: Compare rise time, overshoot, late oscillation and peak motor torque on the same axes.
learning.validation: The high gain must rise faster, add at least 0.1 rad overshoot relative to the low gain, use more peak torque, remain finite and respect the 10 N m limit.
learning.explanation: Explain why greater virtual spring stiffness accelerates the table harder but supplies no new velocity-dependent damping.
learning.transfer: Use proportional position control when modest stiffness is sufficient; the remaining oscillation motivates derivative velocity feedback in Lesson 20.
